segments.name: Vitebsk and Riga: The Disputed Origin

stops.name: Vitebsk, the birth of Guta Israiley
stops.date_confidence: Year only, and given as circa. The UBA Diccionario de musicos judios exiliados en Argentina, vol. I p. 195, gives the birth name Guta Israiley, Vitebsk, circa 1907; Wikidata Q81939577 reads the same. No day or month is recorded anywhere and 1 January is a default for ordering. A birth date of 1 April 1907 circulates attributed to a Yiddish discography site that, on inspection, carries no biographical note on her at all. No birth certificate has been produced.
stops.campa: She is born Guta Israiley in Vitebsk, in the governorate of the same name, a Yiddish-speaking provincial city of the Russian Empire that will be Belarus before she is thirty. No birth certificate has been produced, and her mother is not named in any document consulted. The year reaches us through a dictionary of Jewish musicians exiled to Argentina, compiled in Buenos Aires seven decades later out of arrival papers and theatre programmes. Her father's given name, Zalman, surfaces exactly once, cut into a gravestone at Holon in 1983.

stops.name: Riga, the name Gita Galina
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source dates her arrival in Riga, her training, or her adoption of the stage name. 1928 is chosen to sit inside the Riga-Kovno phase the UBA dictionary frames as 1928-1934 and orders the segment only. The Digital Yiddish Theatre Project essay on Perlman states she was 'also from Riga' and had already made a name for herself; the UBA dictionary and Wikidata both give Vitebsk as her birthplace. The contradiction is left standing. The pin is the Old Town Jewish quarter, not an address.
stops.campa: Two hundred and fifty miles northwest of Vitebsk, on the Baltic, the Yiddish stage of Riga is professional, salaried and busy: the Nayer Yidisher Teater, the dramatic studio of the Peretz Club, directors who move between Riga, Kovno and Warsaw on the same circuit. Guta Israiley becomes Gita Galina somewhere in it, and by the time anyone writes her down she has already made a name. A retrospective written ninety years later says she was a Riga girl herself. The Buenos Aires dictionary says Vitebsk. Nothing settles it.
suggested_refs: The Nayer Yidisher Teater and the Peretz Club dramatic studio, Riga, the two professional entrances to the Latvian Yiddish stage

stops.name: Riga, meeting Max Perelman
stops.date_confidence: Year inferred. The DYTP essay places the meeting in the Riga theatre and gives no date; 1932 is the value already carried in max_perelman.journey.json, derived from the fact that joint touring precedes the London engagement of 1934-35. stops.campa: Max Perelman, born Meiers Perlmanis in this city in 1909, has sung since he was six in Cantor Rozovski's choir and acted professionally since 1928. They meet in the theatre. Which of them was the better known name that year depends on which source is read: one says she had established herself before he came to her, and the dictionary that supplies her birth year says nothing about it either way. From here the two travel as one booking, the same companies and the same steamer tickets, for close to fifty years.

stops.date_confidence: Attested for Perelman, reconstruction for Galina. Zylbercweig's lexicon entry gives '1933-1934 -- in Kovno's Yidish Meutim Theatre' and does not name her. Galina is not named in the sentence that records it. The lexicon carrying the whole of this early period was compiled from the actors' own accounts and it is a Perelman entry; she enters its grammar only as the person he is with. Whether she stood on a Kovno stage cannot be shown from it, and no Lithuanian playbill has been found.

segments.name: The Interwar Circuit: Vienna to Warsaw

stops.name: Vienna, five months at the Reklam Theater
stops.date_confidence: Engagement attested, year not. Zylbercweig gives no date for Vienna; it can only be said to postdate the Kovno seasons of 1933-1934, which the same sentence names immediately before it. June 1934 is a placeholder that orders the circuit. The street address of the Reklam Theatre was not located, so the pin is the corpus's central Vienna coordinate. The quoted wording is the Museum of Family History translator's English, not Zylbercweig's Yiddish, which was not inspected.
stops.campa: The Reklam Theatre engages the company for five months under a director named Goldflis, and here, for the first time in any surviving sentence, Gita Galina is written down beside her husband rather than behind him. It is the only leg of the whole European circuit for which a source names her. Vienna in the middle thirties still has a Yiddish-theatre public and a cabaret grammar the pair will use for the next thirty years: the sketch, the topical song, the married couple playing a married couple.

stops.name: Pavilion Theatre, Whitechapel Road: the London season
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction for Galina. Zylbercweig gives a London season under director Fanny Blumenthal with no year and no theatre; the DYTP essay separately names the Pavilion for a Perlman London engagement. The Pavilion closed in 1935, which bounds the visit, and month and day are ordering defaults. Galina is not named for London in either source. The coordinate is inherited from max_perelman.journey.json, taken from the Survey of London record for the building behind the Whitechapel Road frontage.
stops.campa: The Pavilion on Whitechapel Road is the largest Yiddish playhouse in Britain and has perhaps a year of working life left; it shuts in 1935 and stands empty until it is cleared in 1962. Fanny Blumenthal directs the season. The East End audience is immigrant, Yiddish-first, one boat and one generation from the Baltic, and used to being sung to in its own language by people who arrived the same way. From here the company works north into the provincial towns, where the same audience is smaller and further apart.
suggested_refs: The Pavilion Theatre, 191-193 Whitechapel Road, closed 1935, demolished 1962

stops.name: Liverpool, the provincial circuit begins
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Zylbercweig lists 'Liverpool, Leeds, Glasgow, Manchester' in a single clause about Perelman, with no dates, no venues and no mention of Galina. November 1934 orders the segment after the London season. No notice in any Liverpool paper has been located. City-centre coordinate.
stops.campa: The lexicon gives the British provinces in one breath: Liverpool, Leeds, Glasgow, Manchester. Four words, no theatre named, no date fixed, and no local notice that anyone has turned up since. What the tour was is not in doubt. Two principals and a music case, moving between hired halls and the Jewish institutes of the port cities, playing three nights and packing. Liverpool's Jewish community sits around Brownlow Hill, up the slope from the docks that carried it in.

stops.name: Manchester, the last British stop
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Same single clause of the Zylbercweig entry; Manchester stands here for Leeds and Glasgow as well, which are not given separate stops because nothing distinguishes their evidence. February 1935 is an ordering date. Coordinate inherited from max_perelman.journey.json, where Manchester likewise stands for all four cities.
stops.campa: Cheetham Hill holds the largest Jewish population in England outside London, and it is the natural end of the northern run. Nothing survives of what was played here, or when, or in what hall. The house style is fixed by now: Perelman as the shlimazl who comes right in the last act, Galina as the wife who watches him do it, songs between the scenes, an audience laughing at itself in its own language. Then south again, and across the water to the Continent.

Wikidata Q81939577 lists France among Galina's residences, which is weak independent support and is uncited there. The date orders the segment. Coordinate is the corpus's Paris pin.
stops.campa: Roughly a year in Paris, under three directors the lexicon names as Lachtiger, Lazar and Lustik. For her the year rests on one thing: Wikidata, compiled later from sources nobody has traced, lists France among the countries she lived in. The Yiddish-speaking quarter runs from the rue des Rosiers out to the Belleville workshops, refugees out of Poland and Romania stacked on top of a Jewish population that has been French for a century. The company plays to it, in halls the entry does not name.

stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction throughout. Zylbercweig names only 'Belgium' and a director, Mendelevitsh; no city, no venue, no date, and Galina is not named. stops.campa: The Skala takes them for guest appearances, and after the Skala the rest of Poland: the largest Yiddish-theatre country on earth, three million Jews, a circuit of houses and halls in every provincial town. It is the last leg, and the last season of the world the circuit moved through. Within three years the Skala will stand inside the ghetto wall and its audience will be dead. The couple leave Europe in the spring of 1939 on a theatrical booking, not on a flight from anything.

segments.name: The Oceania and the Compania Israelita de Operetas

stops.name: Trieste, the embarkation for the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: Port attested, date not. The UBA dictionary states that they ARRIVED on 7 June 1939 aboard the Oceania 'habiendo embarcado en Trieste'; the departure itself is undated and May 1939 is a placeholder that orders the crossing before the arrival. Reading 7 June as a sailing date is wrong. The invitation from the impresario Adolf Mide is Zylbercweig's, and is stated for Perelman alone. Coordinate is the Stazione Marittima, inherited from max_perelman.journey.json.
stops.campa: The impresario Adolf Mide has invited Perelman to Argentina, and the pair take ship at Trieste aboard the Oceania, a Cosulich motorship working the run down to the River Plate. The sailing date is nowhere in the record; only the landfall is. The Stazione Marittima in the spring of 1939 is loading two kinds of passenger, contracted performers with return dates and Jews with nothing to return to, and nobody writes down which queue these two stood in or what they thought they were doing.

stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The UBA dictionary records the arrival at vol. I p. 195 for Galina and vol. stops.campa: The Oceania berths on the seventh of June, and the dictionary of exiled musicians takes both names off the same manifest: Gitta Galina and Max Perlmann, embarked at Trieste. It is the one day of her life fixed to the day by a document. Buenos Aires holds something like a quarter of a million Jews, a Yiddish press, half a dozen working stages, and an audience that has been waiting for European stars since the circuit stopped sending them. Three months later Germany invades Poland.

stops.name: Teatro Excelsior, Corrientes 3224: the Abasto house
stops.date_confidence: Affiliation attested, chronology corrected. Zylbercweig reads: 'In 1939 he was invited to Argentina by Adolf Mide, with whom they had acted for three years, then in a member troupe in the Excelsior.' The three years were with Mide's company and the Excelsior engagement follows; a reading that makes 1939-1942 an Excelsior residency is wrong. September 1939 is an ordering date. Address confirmed as Avenida Corrientes 3224, facing the old Abasto market, opened 1912, demolished 1961; Paula Ansaldo places both the Excelsior and the Soleil in Abasto, not on the downtown stretch of Corrientes.
stops.campa: Corrientes 3224, facing the old Abasto market: a house of 1912, pulled down in 1961, one of the two or three Buenos Aires stages on which Yiddish theatre was frankly commercial rather than idealistic. They act three years with Mide's company and then in a troupe at the Excelsior, and Galina joins the Compania Israelita de Operetas. Opereta is the form. Kalman and Offenbach and Straus sung in Yiddish, a soubrette, a comic, an orchestra in the pit, and a public that pays at the door.

stops.name: Teatro Mitre, the house in Villa Crespo
stops.date_confidence: Affiliation attested, date invented. stops.campa: Two theatres carry her name in the Argentine record, and behind them a third: the Mitre, in Villa Crespo, the barrio the Jewish immigration filled first. A scholarly footnote written eighty years later puts it plainly, that his wife Guita Galina was also an actress and singer of the Yiddish theatre, especially of the Mitre and Soleil theatres. No programme from the Mitre naming her has been found, no production, no date. The address of the house itself is not established.

stops.name: Teatro Excelsior, the JKG concert of 9 May 1942
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day on one archival authority. The UBA dictionary gives the date, the venue, the conductor Leo Schwarz and the organising body, the Jewish community's cultural society. This entry was not independently cross-checked against the Buenos Aires German-Jewish press, though the parallel 1943 entry was. Coordinate as for the Corrientes 3224 stop.
stops.campa: Leo Schwarz conducts, the Jewish community's cultural society has organised the evening, and Perelman and Galina are the bill. Date, venue, conductor and sponsor all come from a single line in one archival entry. In Europe that month the deportation trains are running at their fullest. In Buenos Aires the German-Jewish emigration and the older Yiddish-speaking immigration share an audience, an orchestra and a hall, and the entertainment they pay for is the operetta they grew up on.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the photograph in the Argentinisches Tageblatt
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day, unseen. The UBA dictionary records a photograph of Galina in the Argentinisches Tageblatt of 16 September 1943 and does not describe it. It is the only image of Gita Galina that any catalogue consulted records by date, and what it shows is nowhere described, not the dress, not the pose, not whether she is in character. A German-language paper in Argentina in 1943 is read by refugees, and its theatre page is one of the few places left in the world where the life they lost is still being advertised as available for the price of a seat.

stops.name: Montevideo, the river crossed

Zylbercweig adds 'during the summertime in Montevideo, Uruguay' in a sentence about Perelman that does not name her. 1944 orders the segment. Coordinate inherited from max_perelman.journey.json.

Montevideo is an hour across the Plate by boat and holds a Jewish community of its own. Zylbercweig puts Perelman there in the summertime and does not mention her. The porteno summer, when Buenos Aires empties, is when a company crosses.

segments.name: Southern Africa, the Grand Palais, and the Return to Corrientes

stops.name: His Majesty's Theatre, Johannesburg: the first South African season
stops.date_confidence: Season attested with Galina named; the numbers are not. ESAT confirms Perelman starred in Sarah Sylvia's 1948 season of Yiddish theatre at His Majesty's 'with Guita Galina'. The eight-week run and the twenty thousand attendees in a fortnight rest on Veronica Belling alone, and the DYTP essay's figure of 20,000 comes from the same lineage. Some accounts date the first season 1949. Month and day are defaults. Coordinate is the artefacts.co.za record for the building at Commissioner, Eloff, Fox and Joubert Streets, Marshalltown.
stops.campa: Sarah Sylvia, actress and impresario, brings the company out to South Africa, and the season opens at His Majesty's on the corner of Commissioner and Eloff. The Jewish population of the Witwatersrand is Lithuanian almost to a family, a generation off the boat from Kovno and Riga, and what walks onto the stage in front of them is the Baltic Yiddish theatre they left behind, still working and arrived by sea after them. Twenty thousand people are said to come in the first fortnight.
suggested_refs: His Majesty's Theatre, Commissioner and Eloff Streets, Marshalltown, Johannesburg, demolished
sources: ESAT (Encyclopaedia of South African Theatre), via max_perelman.journey.json

stops.name: Johannesburg, the farewell letter of 8 April 1949
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, text not read. The South African Jewish Chronicle of 8 April 1949 is said to carry a joint letter signed 'Max Perlman. Gita Galina'. The archived PDF at ibali.uct.ac.za was fetched but returned image data only, with no extractable text, so the wording rests on a dossier summary and is carried at reconstruction strength. No specific city is fixed for the letter itself and Johannesburg stands for the tour.
stops.campa: The South African Jewish Chronicle of the eighth of April prints a letter of thanks over both their names: to their friends and admirers in the Union of South Africa and Southern Rhodesia, and to Sarah Sylvia for the opportunity to perform there. They are leaving for London, engaged by the actor Meir Tzelniker. Of every paper that survives from her life, from ship manifests to cemetery ledgers, this is the only one said to carry her own signature, and the archived page of it has never been rendered legibly enough for anyone to read the wording. She signs it second.
suggested_refs: South African Jewish Chronicle, 8 April 1949, the Perlman and Galina farewell letter, archived at ibali.uct.ac.za

stops.name: The Grand Palais, London: the Tzelniker engagement
stops.date_confidence: Season attested, month not. The DYTP essay gives Grand Palais engagements in 1949, 1951 and 1955 with the titles 'Here Comes Grandpa', 'The Shlemmazl' and 'The American Litvak'; no months are given and June is an ordering default. The Tzelniker engagement comes from the couple's own 1949 letter, whose text could not be read. The pin approximates the Commercial Road stretch of the East End Yiddish theatre district and is roughly 600 m from the theatre's address at 133 Commercial Road; it should not be read as the building.
stops.campa: 133 Commercial Road, the last working Yiddish theatre in Britain, run by the Tzelniker family, and Meir Tzelniker has engaged them off the strength of the African season. There will be three Grand Palais seasons, 1949, 1951 and 1955, and the surviving titles are Here Comes Grandpa, The Shlemmazl and The American Litvak. stops.name: Li-La-Lo, the Yasha Heifetz Hall: programme twenty-five
stops.date_confidence: Date reconstructed and the venue corrected. Rachel Rojanski's Yiddish in Israel is the source for Galina in programme 25, Zehirut ha-derekh be-tikun, premiering 31 October 1953 with Ann Crawley and Rosa Turkov; the book was not opened in any pass. Circumstantial support: Perelman told reporters on 12-13 November that they had been in the country two weeks, implying arrival around 29 October, and Li-La-Lo mounted 26 programmes in all, closing with Haleluia in February 1954. The dossier's 'Matate/Li-La-Lo, political-satirical' fuses two separate companies: HaMatate was the satirical theatre; Li-La-Lo, founded 1944 by Moshe Valin, staged escapist European cabaret. Coordinate is the Yasha Heifetz Hall on Simtat HaShoeva off Allenby, later the Matmid cinema, and is approximate.
stops.campa: Li-La-Lo, founded by the impresario Moshe Valin in 1944, plays European cabaret in Hebrew off Allenby Street, in a hall on Simtat HaShoeva that will end its life as a cinema. It mounts twenty-six programmes in ten years and shuts in 1954. Galina appears in one of the last, Zehirut ha-derekh be-tikun, opening the thirty-first of October, alongside Ann Crawley and Rosa Turkov. She has been in the country about two days. She is performing in Hebrew, which is not her language.

stops.name: Dizengoff Square, the car in the fountain
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Eli Alon's retrospective in News1 confirms the incident in detail: two in the morning of 13 November 1953, after the Thursday night performance of 12 November, the impresario at the wheel, Perelman and his wife Guita Galina aboard, light scratches only, the driver blaming the darkness. The site returns 403 to direct fetch and renders through a text proxy; an earlier pass that reported the story unverifiable was wrong and that verdict is withdrawn. The photograph attributed to Hans Pinn has not been located.
stops.campa: Thursday night's performance ends late. At two in the morning a car with the impresario at the wheel, Max Perelman and Galina inside, drives into the fountain at Dizengoff Square. Everybody climbs out scratched. The driver blames the dark. Perelman tells the reporters that they have been in the country two weeks and have already been given a nice and respectable bath at Dizengoff Square. The photograph taken that night is the reason the story is still in print seventy years on.

stops.campa: The second name on the advertised route. Jerusalem that January is a divided city, the armistice line running through it, and the Yiddish question is politically live: the young state's cultural authorities tax and discourage Yiddish performance as a rival to Hebrew, and the company is working in both languages inside the same season, Hebrew cabaret at Li-La-Lo and Yiddish comedy on the road. Nothing at all is known about the Jerusalem night, not the hall, not the bill, not the house. A newspaper said there would be one.

stops.campa: They found their own Yiddish company, the Comedy Theatre, and run it on melodrama and musical comedy: Der groyser fardiner, Shlimazl, Motl Mayers glikn, Der yidisher gazlen, Alts tsulib parnose. The last title means everything for a living, which is also the business model. Yiddish is taxed and discouraged in the young state, and they open a Yiddish house anyway. One historian's archival work is the whole basis for the founding. Another account describes the same year as a nine-month visit and mentions no company at all.

stops.name: The Grand Palais, London: The Shlemazzel reviewed
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day, and the attribution corrected. The review is A.B.L., 'Entertainments. Theatre. The Shlemazzel', Jewish Chronicle (London), 4 February 1955, p. 24, quoted with its footnote in the DYTP essay and fetched directly. max_perelman.journey.json attaches the same sentence to the 1948 Johannesburg season; the DYTP footnote is explicit that it is London, 1955, and the contradiction is left standing rather than resolved. stops.campa: The Jewish Chronicle sends a critic signed A.B.L. down to Commercial Road, and on the fourth of February prints his notice. Almost all of it is about Perelman: the worm who turns, the shlimazl who comes good, the clowning and the dancing. One clause is about her. It is the only sentence written by a contemporary that describes what Gita Galina actually did on a stage, and it describes her charming, singing, playing, and married. She has been a professional actress for close to thirty years.
stops.quote: It matters little that it is not very original or convincing, the important thing being its suitability as a vehicle for the antics of this most likeable comedian. He is a worm who turns, a shlemazzel who becomes successful, and the clowning, singing and dancing in which he indulges in the process are most entertaining. Guita Galina contributes some charming singing and playing as his wife.
stops.quote_source: A.B.L., 'Entertainments. Theatre. The Shlemazzel,' Jewish Chronicle (London), 4 February 1955, p. 24, quoted at footnote 19 of the Digital Yiddish Theatre Project essay on Max Perlman
